title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks; 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks), a single generator/prompt pairing (requested model: gpt-5-mini), and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applying the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Two preregistration/execution issues affect interpretation: (1) shared-generation semantics removed the per-arm stochasticity assumed by the preregistered power calculation, and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR provided no additional verifier-detectable benefit in this executed artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred; results do not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, repair budget, or verifier.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) promise to accelerate network operations by translating high-level human intent into low-level device configuration. However, stochastic generation can produce syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect configurations that violate operational invariants (reachability, required workflow sequences, protected interfaces). Prior systems and operator guidance therefore recommend interposing deterministic validators and iterative repair (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects before execution. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (study c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) to test whether bounded GVR (a deterministic verifier plus at most one bounded LLM repair attempt) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations relative to an unconstrained LLM baseline (and, prespecified, relative to a schema-constrained baseline). The study used a synthetic NetOps task bank of 240 paired tasks, a single generator/prompt pairing (requested model gpt-5-mini), and a deterministic validator that emits structured diagnostics. The preregistration, analysis executor, and execution manifest were frozen prior to observing results and form the authoritative record for this run.
sections.related_work: Three literature streams frame this work. First, empirical studies document LLM hallucinations and incorrect outputs for code and structured artifacts, establishing that unconstrained generation may produce plausible but incorrect artifacts that fail deeper invariants (surveys and case studies summarized in the evidence synthesis). Second, methods work on generate–verify–repair, constrained decoding, and grammar/schema enforcement shows that interposing validators or explicit-decoding constraints improves mechanically checkable properties (syntactic validity, compilability, schema compliance). These studies support the architectural plausibility of GVR but also emphasize that gains on surface metrics do not automatically imply domain-level semantic correctness for complex NetOps invariants. Third, systems and NetOps research advocate verifier-driven pipelines and intent-based translation frameworks that combine LLMs with topology-aware verification; prototypes commonly recommend human oversight for high-stakes changes. The supplied literature synthesis (established findings C1–C6 and candidate gaps G1–G3) underscores two practical tensions: validator completeness (oracle coverage) and the need for evaluation semantics that preserve generator stochasticity when assessing repair efficacy.
sections.methodology: Preregistered estimand and hypotheses. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed by a frozen analysis executor; the preregistration specified Bonferroni correction across two primary comparisons and a fixed-N design (N = 240 pairs). The two prespecified primary hypotheses were: H1—GVR reduces verifier-detected violations versus unconstrained generation; H2—GVR reduces violations versus schema-constrained decoding. Study implementation. The adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed the preregistered contract. Requested generator: gpt-5-mini. Critical executed runtime parameters recorded in the execution manifest were generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 (single bounded repair). The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied the full_intent_constraint_validation rule: checks include required command sequences, topology-aware reachability, protected-interface preservation, and final-state predicates; it returns structured traces (violation_count, violation list, normalized_configuration, and difficulty metadata). Task bank. The public synthetic task bank contains 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks = 240 tasks; each task encodes an initial device state, a natural-language intent, workflow constraints (required_sequence), and an expected final state. Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, level) is used by the validator in producing structured validation traces. Analysis plan. The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) performed an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired outcomes and computed absolute risk reductions with paired-bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness rules and conservative sensitivity analyses were preregistered. Critical execution deviations. Two prespecified elements of the preregistration were not realized in this artifact-backed run: (1) the adapter-configured execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per task reused across arms), which removes within-pair stochasticity; and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline paired experiment was not executed in the archived run and therefore is absent from the confirmatory outputs.

sections.discussion: Conservative scientific interpretation. In the executed setting (single generator/prompt pairing, shared-initial-candidate semantics, synthetic task bank, single bounded repair attempt, deterministic verifier), bounded GVR produced no verifier-detectable benefit because there were no verifier-detectable errors to correct. This null outcome is artifact-backed and must be interpreted with the execution semantics in mind: with shared-generation the two arms observed the same generated candidate per task, precluding discordance-driven detection of repair utility. Design lessons for future evaluations. Two evaluation choices determine sensitivity to GVR benefits: (1) generation semantics—independent per-condition generation is required when the scientific goal is to measure GVR’s capacity to correct stochastic generator errors; shared-generation reduces model-call cost but also removes within-pair stochasticity and thus statistical power for paired tests; and (2) verifier sensitivity and task selection—the task bank plus golden/reference injections must produce verifier-detectable failures at non-negligible rates to observe effect sizes. The preregistration included a 10% golden-task injection plan and adversarial checks to validate verifier sensitivity; those golden injections were not realized in the archived adapter-configured run. Practical recommendations (evidence-grounded). To restore the preregistered inferential assumptions and robustly evaluate GVR we recommend (a) rerunning the frozen task bank with independent_condition_generation = true (the execution manifest records generation seeds so reruns are reproducible under independent generation), (b) injecting adversarial/golden tasks per the preregistered 10% plan to validate verifier sensitivity, (c) expanding generator scope to multi-model regimes, and (d) increasing the repair budget and exploring iterative repair strategies to assess multi-iteration convergence behavior. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the executed shared-generation semantics violated the preregistered independent-generation assumption and removed discordance potential, invalidating the preregistered power calculation for detecting a 10-percentage-point paired reduction. Construct validity: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of operational risks outside the verifier’s encoded invariants (oracle incompleteness risk). External validity: synthetic tasks, one model (gpt-5-mini), and a single repair budget limit generalization. Conclusion validity: zero discordant outcomes preclude evidence that bounded GVR changes verifier-detectable rates under the executed semantics. Operational implication. The artifact-backed null result emphasizes that evaluation semantics, verifier coverage, and adversarial task selection determine whether GVR benefits are measurable; designers of operational pipelines must therefore align verifier completeness and evaluation semantics with the intended operational claims for repair loops.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact-archived paired experiment evaluating bounded GVR for intent→configuration NetOps on a public synthetic task bank. Under the executed shared-generation semantics every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier (n11 = 240), yielding a degenerate null paired estimate (0.0), exact McNemar p = 1.00, and paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR did not add verifier-detectable value in this artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred. Two preregistration/execution deviations constrain inference: (1) shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption; and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed and the archived artifacts contain no recorded rationale. We release the authoritative archived artifacts so others can reproduce the accounting and extend the evaluation under independent-generation, adversarial/golden-task injections, multi-model regimes, and expanded verifier coverage to more robustly assess GVR’s operational value.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
